claims.statement: While his band was trading at a Mexican town the Apaches called Kas-ki-yeh, Mexican troops attacked the camp; when he returned he found that his aged mother, his young wife and his three small children were among the dead. His own account dates this to the summer of 1858; the National Archives gives 1851 and the Oklahoma Historical Society 1850.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The killings are documented; the year is disputed. The anchor for the synthetic traumatic grief and post-traumatic stress in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In his own words, that night he stood alone by the river, did not vote in the council, had no weapon and hardly wished to fight, and 'had no purpose left'; on the march home he did not eat and spoke to no one. At home he burned his family's belongings, vowed vengeance, and wrote that he was never again contented in his quiet home.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own description of grief, recorded as history. It is not a retrospective diagnosis; the modern episode's assessment of grief and post-traumatic stress is synthetic. Under Apache custom the property of deceased relatives was not kept, so burning their belongings is mourning practice, not a symptom.

source_links.locator: I did not pray, nor did I resolve to do anything in particular, for I had no purpose left; I spoke to no one and no one spoke to me; I burned them all, even our tepee; I was never again contented in our quiet home; According to custom he should not have kept the property of his deceased relatives

claims.statement: He listed eight wounds received in his wars with Mexican forces, among them a gunshot to the right leg above the knee (the bullet still carried), a gunshot through the left forearm, a saber wound below the right knee, a blow to the top of the head with a musket butt that knocked him senseless, a shot just below the outer corner of the left eye, and shots in the left side and the back.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the past medical history of combat wounds and a head injury with loss of consciousness, and the retained bullet; no lasting effect of these wounds is documented.

The promise that the men would see their families in Florida was not kept: he and his warriors were held at Fort Pickens, at hard labor sawing logs, and did not see their families until May 1887.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the documented imprisonment and separation from family in the trauma-informed history.

claims.statement: As prisoners of war the Chiricahua Apache were held in Florida, then at Mount Vernon in Alabama, and from 1894 at Fort Sill; many died of malaria in Florida, many children died of tuberculosis in Alabama, and only 119 remained when they were moved to Oklahoma. In his words, so many of his people died in Alabama that he let one of his wives go to the Mescalero Agency.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the collective losses in captivity in the trauma-informed history.

claims.statement: He died at Fort Sill on February 17, 1909, of pneumonia. On a cold February day he had ridden into Lawton and obtained whisky; returning after nightfall he fell from his horse and lay until morning near his house, partly in water. He was taken to the post hospital and died days later, aged 79 by his own reckoning, and was buried in the Apache cemetery at Fort Sill.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Chronic post-traumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder in a 77-year-old Chiricahua Apache elder who has lived for twenty years under federal custody far from his homeland, seen at a tribal health clinic near Fort Sill. The episode covers trauma-informed, culturally safe care with an interpreter, his own words and choices first, and traditional healing offered alongside clinic care without probing his beliefs, as the Indian Health Service policy asks; screening with the PC-PTSD-5, the PCL-5 and the AUDIT, and confirmation with the CAPS-5 interview under the VA/DoD 1903 and APA 1897 PTSD guidelines; telling grief apart from prolonged grief disorder by DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural norms, without turning mourning into a diagnosis; a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; cognitive processing therapy adapted for an older man who does not read English; sertraline at a low dose with a sodium check; why prazosin was not started in an older man who had fallen, although the VA/DoD guideline suggests it for nightmares; no benzodiazepines; naltrexone with liver and kidney checks and acamprosate as the alternative; fall risk, and pneumococcal, high-dose influenza, RSV, zoster and Tdap vaccines at his age.

referral.question: Years of poor sleep, nightmares and unwanted memories, with heavy drinking at night, in a Chiricahua Apache elder of 77 who lost his mother, wife and children to violence when young, fought for decades and has lived twenty years in federal custody. Please confirm or exclude post-traumatic stress disorder with a structured interview, help us tell his grief apart from prolonged grief disorder, and advise on therapy and medicines that suit his age, his language and his drinking

referral.pertinent_history: First language Chiricahua Apache, with Spanish and some English; does not read English; seen with the clinic's Apache interpreter. Sleeps three or four hours with nightmares most nights; unwanted memories by day; startles easily; avoids talking of the past. PC-PTSD-5 5, PCL-5 56, PHQ-9 11 with item 9 scored 0, Mini-Cog 4. AUDIT 19: four or more drinks most evenings to sleep; four DSM-5-TR criteria for alcohol use disorder; no past withdrawal seizures or delirium. A fall a month ago walking home after drinking, bruised left hip; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds. Old wounds, including a head injury with loss of consciousness long ago. MCV 101 fL; AST 58, ALT 36 and GGT 112 U/L; albumin and bilirubin normal; creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 78); B12 and TSH normal; PEth 236 ng/mL. Thiamine started. A structured safety assessment found no suicidal thoughts; he has no firearm; safety plan and 988 card given. He wants to sleep without the dead coming back to him and does not want whisky to rule his nights

consultant_note.history: Geronimo, a Chiricahua Apache elder of 77, is seen with the clinic interpreter at the request of Dr. Whitehorse-Lindgren. He asked to be called Geronimo. He told me, in his own words and only as far as he chose, that as a young man he came back to his camp to find his mother, his wife and his three children killed by soldiers, that he fought for many years afterwards, and that since his surrender he and his people have been held far from their country. For many years he has slept badly; the killings and old battles come back in dreams most nights and in his mind by day, he wakes ready to fight, he startles at sudden sounds, and he keeps away from talk of the past. He drinks whisky at night to sleep and has cut down since intake. He has not thought of ending his life. He grieves his family and his people, and he said that this grief is his and is kept in the way his people keep it
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Whitehorse-Lindgren's intake note, safety assessment and safety plan. PC-PTSD-5 5, PCL-5 56 at intake and 54 today, PHQ-9 11, AUDIT 19, Mini-Cog 4. Blood count with MCV 101 fL; AST 58, ALT 36, GGT 112 U/L; albumin and bilirubin normal; creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, eGFR 78; sodium 139 mmol/L; B12 and TSH normal; PEth 236 ng/mL. Urine test today negative for opioids. Blood pressure today 134/78, pulse 78

exam.finding: Alert and composed; dignified and watchful; speech measured through the interpreter; mood tired; affect restricted; startles at a door closing; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; insight and judgment good
No tremor; steady gait

assessment.assessment: On the CAPS-5 he meets criteria in all four symptom clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative changes in thinking and mood, and arousal), with a severity score of 44, lasting decades and impairing his sleep and daily life. The diagnosis is chronic post-traumatic stress disorder, rooted in the killing of his family, years of combat and captivity. His Mini-Cog of 4 does not suggest dementia; cognition should be rechecked once he sleeps better and drinks less

Prolonged grief disorder requires, nearly every day for at least the past month, intense yearning for or preoccupation with the dead with further symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief or intense emotional pain, beyond what his culture would expect. His grief is lasting and deep but is not that daily, consuming yearning, and the way he mourns follows the customs of his people. The criteria are not met. His grief should be respected as grief, not treated as a disorder; the distress that brings him in is driven by the post-traumatic symptoms

The VA/DoD guideline recommends an individual, manualized trauma-focused psychotherapy (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure or EMDR) over medicine, and the APA guideline strongly recommends cognitive processing therapy and prolonged exposure. Cognitive processing therapy suits him: it can be given without the written trauma account, its worksheets can be done aloud through an interpreter, and it does not require him to retell the killings in detail, which he has said he will not do. For a man of 77: a steady pace, shorter sessions when he tires, a consistent interpreter, and video sessions when he cannot come in, which the guideline supports. The therapist should ask how he wishes to speak of those who died and follow his lead

Sertraline, paroxetine and venlafaxine are recommended by the VA/DoD guideline; the APA guideline suggests fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline and venlafaxine. Paroxetine is best avoided at his age because of its anticholinergic effects. If he wants a medicine, sertraline 25 mg rising to 50 mg is my choice, with sodium checked within the first month because SSRIs can lower sodium in older adults, and attention to bleeding and falls. Benzodiazepines should not be used. The VA/DoD guideline suggests prazosin for nightmares associated with PTSD, though not for PTSD as a whole; in a man of 77 who has just fallen and is drinking, its first-dose and standing drops in blood pressure outweigh the benefit for now. Reconsider it, with standing pressures, if nightmares persist after therapy

I agree with four DSM-5-TR criteria. The VA/DoD guideline advises that a substance use disorder should not delay trauma-focused therapy, so both are treated together. Naltrexone suits him: AST is under three times the upper limit, his kidneys are normal, and he takes no opioids; liver tests should be repeated at four to six weeks. Acamprosate, dosed by kidney function, is the alternative if naltrexone cannot be used. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium and has cut down without symptoms, so no withdrawal medicine is needed
